claim: S. mansoni is impacted by cattle and wild vertebrates because of their role in supporting trematode parasites, the larvae of which have antagonistic interactions with S. mansoni in their shared Biomphalaria vector snails.
source: We show S. mansoni is impacted by cattle and wild vertebrates because of their role in supporting trematode parasites, the larvae of which have antagonistic interactions with S. mansoni in their shared Biomphalaria vector snails.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing interactions between trematode species in snails, field survey data showing co-occurrence of multiple trematode species, and experimental exposures demonstrating antagonistic effects.

claim: The abundant cattle trematode, Calicophoron sukari, fails to develop in Biomphalaria pfeifferi unless S. mansoni larvae are present in the same snail.
source: We discovered the abundant cattle trematode, Calicophoron sukari, fails to develop in Biomphalaria pfeifferi unless S. mansoni larvae are present in the same snail.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental exposure data showing C. sukari has very low infection success when exposed alone (0.68-1.3% prevalence) compared to when co-exposed with S. mansoni, and histological evidence showing undeveloped C. sukari sporocysts surrounded by hemocytes.

claim: Further development of S. mansoni is subsequently prevented by C. sukari's presence.
source: Further development of S. mansoni is subsequently prevented by C. sukari's presence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing significantly reduced S. mansoni shedding prevalence in co-exposure experiments, particularly when C. sukari was introduced before or simultaneously with S. mansoni.

claim: Removal of C. sukari would increase S. mansoni-infected snails by two-fold.
source: Modeling indicated that removal of C. sukari would increase S. mansoni-infected snails by two-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling parameterized with empirical data from field surveys and experimental exposures.

claim: Predictable exploitation of aquatic habitats by humans and their cattle enable C. sukari to exploit S. mansoni, thereby limiting transmission of this human pathogen.
source: Predictable exploitation of aquatic habitats by humans and their cattle enable C. sukari to exploit S. mansoni, thereby limiting transmission of this human pathogen.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from field observations showing co-occurrence of both parasites in areas where humans and cattle share water sources, combined with experimental data showing the facilitation-antagonism relationship.

claim: The Lake Victoria Basin is one of the largest hyperendemic areas of schistosomiasis in the world.
source: S. mansoni is the most geographically widespread causative agent of intestinal schistosomiasis, and the Lake Victoria Basin is one of the largest hyperendemic areas of schistosomiasis in the world (Gouvras et al., 2017; Wiegand et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Children living in villages near the lakeshore often exhibit prevalence of S. mansoni infection of >50%, and up to 90% in some areas.
source: Despite repeated treatments with the anthelmintic praziquantel, children living in villages near the lakeshore often exhibit prevalence of S. mansoni infection of >50%, and up to 90% in some areas (Woodhall et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A total of 19 species of trematodes were found among 19,914 B. pfeifferi from the perennial Asao Stream with overall prevalence of 12.3%.
source: A total of 19 species were found among 19,914 B. pfeifferi (overall prevalence 12.3%) from the perennial Asao Stream
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data collected from January 2014 to January 2018.

claim: 7 species of trematodes were found from 1,136 B. pfeifferi (15.5% prevalence) from the highly seasonal Kasabong stream.
source: 7 species from 1,136 B. pfeifferi (15.5%) from the highly seasonal Kasabong stream
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data.

claim: 21 species of cercariae were found from 3,369 B. sudanica (10.3% prevalence) from Lake Victoria.
source: from Lake Victoria, 21 species of cercariae from 3,369 B. sudanica (10.3%)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data.

claim: In aggregate, 29 trematode taxa were recovered from the study sites.
source: Some species, like S. mansoni, were recovered from all habitats, but many were habitat specific, such that in aggregate, 29 taxa were recovered.
evidence: This claim is supported by field survey data and molecular identification of trematode species.

claim: All three taxa of Biomphalaria were susceptible to S. mansoni, but B. pfeifferi was the most compatible.
source: A portion of the field-collected Biomphalaria were also exposed to S. mansoni to assess compatibility and we found that all three taxa of Biomphalaria were susceptible to S. mansoni, but found that B. pfeifferi was the most compatible (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental exposure data showing different infection success rates among the three Biomphalaria taxa, with results shown in Figure 1d.

claim: At Asao, C. sukari was the most common trematode recovered from B. pfeifferi (1,035/2439 total infections, or 42.4% of all infections).
source: At Asao and Kasabong, the most common trematode recovered from B. pfeifferi was the cattle-transmitted amphistome Calicophoron sukari (Laidemitt et al., 2017) (1,035/2439 total infections, or 42.4% of all infections at Asao
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data from Asao Stream.

claim: At Kasabong, C. sukari comprised 97/176 infections, or 55.1% of all infections.
source: and at Kasabong 97/176, or 55.1% of all infections
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data from Kasabong stream.

claim: S. mansoni comprised 1014 of 2439 total infections at Asao or 41.6% of all infections.
source: followed closely by S. mansoni (1014 of 2439 total infections at Asao or 41.6% of all infections
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data from Asao Stream.

claim: At Kasabong, S. mansoni comprised 68/176 or 38.6% of all infections.
source: and at Kasabong, 68/176 or 38.6% of all infections
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data from Kasabong stream.

claim: C. sukari was not recovered from B. sudanica or B. choanomphala.
source: Both species were also commonly recovered from B. pfeifferi, but C. sukari was not recovered from B. sudanica or B. choanomphala.
evidence: This claim is supported by field survey data showing absence of C. sukari in these two Biomphalaria species.

claim: The overall prevalence of S. mansoni infections at stream sites (5.09% and 5.89%) was much higher than from the lakeshore (0.22%).
source: Also noteworthy is the overall prevalence of S. mansoni infections at stream sites (5.09% and 5.89%) was much higher than from the lakeshore (0.22%).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by field survey data comparing stream and lakeshore sites.

claim: S. mansoni occupies an intermediate position in the dominance hierarchy at Asao Stream.
source: By observing natural takeover events (Biomphalaria shedding one type of cercariae and then later shedding a different type of cercariae only) and through experimental infections, we discovered that at Asao Stream S. mansoni occupies an intermediate position in the hierarchy
evidence: This claim is supported by both observational data of natural takeover events and experimental superinfection studies.

claim: Echinostomes and C. sukari were the more dominant species than S. mansoni in the hierarchy.
source: and echinostomes and C. sukari were the more dominant species (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental superinfection data and natural takeover observations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Field-derived B. pfeifferi not shedding cercariae at collection were almost as likely to subsequently shed C. sukari as S. mansoni cercariae after exposure to S. mansoni miracidia (p<0.001).
source: We discovered that if B. pfeifferi from stream habitats that were not shedding cercariae of any kind at the time of collection were then exposed to S. mansoni miracidia, surprisingly they were almost as likely to subsequently shed C. sukari as S. mansoni cercariae (p<0.001) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental exposure data with statistical analysis showing significant results.

claim: Control snails not exposed to S. mansoni were subsequently much less likely to shed cercariae of either species.
source: Control snails, otherwise similar except not exposed to S. mansoni, were subsequently much less likely to shed cercariae of either species.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental control group data.

claim: In control experiments with S. mansoni only, peak S. mansoni shedding was 7 weeks post exposure at 86.7% (92/106 surviving B. pfeifferi).
source: In control experiments, peak S. mansoni shedding was 7 weeks post exposure (86.7%, 92/106 surviving B. pfeifferi)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental exposure data.

claim: In control experiments with C. sukari only, peak C. sukari shedding was at 8 weeks post exposure at 0.68% (1/114 surviving B. pfeifferi).
source: and peak C. sukari shedding was at 8 weeks post exposure (0.68%, 1/114 surviving B. pfeifferi).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental exposure data showing very low infection success of C. sukari alone.

claim: In the 'Sm first then two weeks later Cs' experiment, 24.2% (16/66) surviving B. pfeifferi shed S. mansoni and 21.2% (14/66) shed C. sukari cercariae.
source: In the experiment 'Sm first then two weeks later Cs,' 24.2% (16/66) surviving B. pfeifferi shed S. mansoni and 21.2% (14/66) shed C. sukari cercariae.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental co-exposure data.

claim: In the 'Cs then two weeks later Sm' experiment, 35.1% (26/74) of surviving B. pfeifferi shed C. sukari and 2.7% (2/74) shed S. mansoni cercariae.
source: In the experiment 'Cs then two weeks later Sm,' 35.1% (26/74) of surviving B. pfeifferi shed C. sukari and 2.7% (2/74) shed S. mansoni cercariae.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental co-exposure data showing C. sukari dominance when introduced first.

claim: In the simultaneous exposure experiment, 9.2% (7/76) surviving B. pfeifferi shed S. mansoni and 15.8% (12/76) shed C. sukari cercariae.
source: In the simultaneous experiment 9.2% (7/76) surviving B. pfeifferi shed S. mansoni and 15.8% (12/76) shed C. sukari cercariae.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental co-exposure data.

claim: S. mansoni miracidia were capable of infecting B. pfeifferi on their own as expected.
source: The results demonstrated that S. mansoni miracidia were capable of infecting B. pfeifferi on their own as expected (Mutuku et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: C. sukari miracidia were poorly infective to B. pfeifferi on their own.
source: but C. sukari miracidia were poorly infective to B. pfeifferi on their own.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental exposure data showing very low infection rates (0.68-1.3%) in control groups exposed only to C. sukari.

claim: The prevalence of B. pfeifferi shedding S. mansoni was significantly less in the simultaneous (p=0.0478) and 'Cs then two weeks later Sm' experiments (p=0.0292) compared to S. mansoni controls.
source: From these co-exposure experiments the prevalence of B. pfeifferi shedding S. mansoni was significantly less than in the simultaneous (p=0.0478) and 'Cs then two weeks later Sm' experiments (p=0.0292) compared to S. mansoni controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: C. sukari prevalence was significantly higher (p=0.0192) in the 'Cs then two weeks later Sm group'.
source: In comparison, C. sukari prevalence was significantly higher (p=0.0192) in the 'Cs then two weeks later Sm group'.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Histological sections of B. pfeifferi taken 8 days after exposure to only C. sukari miracidia revealed the presence of sporocysts that had undergone little or no growth or development and had host hemocytes around them.
source: Examination of histological sections of B. pfeifferi taken 8 days after exposure to only C. sukari miracidia revealed the presence of sporocysts that had undergone little or no growth or development and had host hemocytes around them (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: S. mansoni sporocysts were much larger at 8 days post-exposure than C. sukari sporocysts and germinal development was underway.
source: By contrast, S. mansoni sporocysts were much larger at the same age and germinal development was underway (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological examination data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The success of C. sukari sporocysts in B. pfeifferi increased significantly (p=<0.0192) if S. mansoni miracidia were also allowed to infect the snails, particularly so if the S. mansoni exposures followed the exposure of snails to C. sukari.
source: The success of C. sukari sporocysts in B. pfeifferi increased significantly (p=<0.0192) if S. mansoni miracidia were also allowed to infect the snails, particularly so if the S. mansoni exposures followed the exposure of snails to C. sukari.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental co-exposure data with statistical analysis.

claim: The increased success of C. sukari in co-infections was accompanied by a sharp reduction in the number of snails shedding S. mansoni cercariae as compared to the snails exposed just to S. mansoni.
source: Importantly, this was accompanied by a sharp reduction in the number of snails shedding S. mansoni cercariae as compared to the snails exposed just to S. mansoni (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Double infections (snails simultaneously shedding cercariae of both S. mansoni and C. sukari species) were rare, and occurred less than expected by chance (p=<0.001).
source: A further indication of the antagonistic interactions between the two trematode species was provided by the observation that although infections of both S. mansoni and C. sukari were common in B. pfeifferi in west Kenyan stream habitats, double infections (snails simultaneously shedding cercariae of both species) were rare, and occurred less than expected by chance (p=<0.001) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by field survey data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Numbers of S. mansoni and C. sukari infections were positively correlated (r = 0.622).
source: Lastly, our survey data also showed that numbers of S. mansoni and C. sukari infections were positively correlated (r = 0.622) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by field survey data with correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The mathematical model predicts that the force of infection of S. mansoni, as measured by the proportion of cercariae-producing (shedding) snails, is reduced by approximately half in the presence of the antagonist C. sukari.
source: The model predicts that the force of infection of S. mansoni, as measured by the proportion of cercariae-producing (shedding) snails, is reduced by approximately half in the presence of the antagonist C. sukari (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling parameterized with empirical data, with results shown in Figure 5a.

claim: If C. sukari were absent then the prevalence of S. mansoni shedders in streams would increase by 50% or more.
source: Therefore, our survey results (Figure 2c) suggest that if C. sukari were absent then the prevalence of S. mansoni shedders in streams would increase by 50% or more.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from survey data and modeling results.

claim: The model predictions highlight that, dependent on the background levels of infection, there may be increases of several hundred percent of S. mansoni cercariae in the absence of C. sukari.
source: Also, the model predictions highlight that, dependent on the background levels of infection, there may be increases of several hundred percent of S. mansoni cercariae in the absence of C. sukari.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results.

claim: Humans are the most important definitive host in maintaining S. mansoni transmission.
source: With respect to mammalian definitive hosts, humans are certainly the most important in maintaining transmission (Colley et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Baboons and common rodents like Mastomys natalensis can also play a role in S. mansoni transmission and may assume greater significance in ongoing chemotherapy-based control programs targeting human transmission.
source: but baboons and common rodents like Mastomys natalensis can also play a role and may assume greater significance in ongoing chemotherapy-based control programs targeting human transmission (Hanelt et al., 2010; Catalano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: S. mansoni in and around Lake Victoria infects three Biomphalaria taxa that exist in different habitats: B. pfeifferi in streams and small impoundments, B. sudanica along the lakeshore, and B. choanomphala in deeper water.
source: Likewise, S. mansoni in and around the lake also infects three Biomphalaria taxa that exist in different habitats. Schistosoma mansoni eggs are passed into aquatic habitats in human feces. A miracidium hatches from an egg and if successful in finding and penetrating a Biomphalaria snail, then initiates a long-term, proliferative period of asexual development. This development culminates in the production of human-infective cercariae which are released or 'shed' into the surrounding water. These obligatory vector hosts include B. pfeifferi in streams and small impoundments, B. sudanica along the lakeshore, and B. choanomphala, now generally considered to be a distinct ecophenotype of B. sudanica, found especially but not exclusively in deeper water (Magendantz, 1972; Standley et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and field observations.

claim: All three Biomphalaria species (B. pfeifferi, B. sudanica, and B. choanomphala) have been found naturally infected with S. mansoni.
source: All three species have been found naturally infected with S. mansoni, (Magendantz, 1972; Standley et al., 2011; Mutuku et al., 2017; Mutuku et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature including field studies.

claim: Rediae possess a mouth surrounded by a powerful sucker, and a gut.
source: Some like S. mansoni develop sac-like sporocysts, whereas others produce rediae possessing a mouth surrounded by a powerful sucker, and a gut (Schell, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established parasitology literature describing trematode morphology.

claim: Rediae can move within the snail and may ingest host tissue, including gonadal tissue.
source: Rediae can move within the snail and may ingest host tissue, including gonadal tissue (Lim and Lie, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The rediae of echinostomes tend to be dominant in intramolluscan interactions, with some echinostome species able to produce small, motile rediae specialized for attacking and killing larvae of other trematodes species, including S. mansoni sporocysts.
source: For example, the rediae of echinostomes (Echinostomatoidea) in particular tend to be dominant in intramolluscan interactions, with some echinostome species able to produce small, motile rediae specialized for attacking and killing larvae of other trematodes species, including S. mansoni sporocysts (Lim and Heyneman, 1972; Moravec et al., 1974; Hechinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on trematode interactions.

claim: Amphistome trematodes produce rediae, and these tend to have more complex antagonistic or facilitation interactions with other trematodes.
source: Amphistome trematodes (Paramphistomoidea) also produce rediae, and these tend to have more complex antagonistic or facilitation interactions with other trematodes (Southgate et al., 1989; Spatz et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Sporocyst-producing species including strigeids and schistosomes have more subtle indirect antagonistic effects on larvae of other trematodes mediated by as yet uncharacterized soluble factors.
source: Sporocyst-producing species including strigeids and schistosomes have also been shown to have more subtle indirect antagonistic effects on larvae of other trematodes mediated by as yet uncharacterized soluble factors (Basch et al., 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Amphistomes of domestic ruminants like C. sukari were more commonly recovered from B. pfeifferi from stream sites whereas echinostomes, mostly transmitted by birds, were more likely to be recovered from B. sudanica from the lakeshore.
source: In general, amphistomes of domestic ruminants like C. sukari were more commonly recovered from B. pfeifferi from stream sites whereas echinostomes, mostly transmitted by birds (Laidemitt et al., 2019), were more likely to be recovered from B. sudanica from the lakeshore.
evidence: This claim is supported by field survey data and citation.

claim: C. sukari relies on S. mansoni for its own transmission.
source: This is not surprising, since C. sukari relies on S. mansoni for its own transmission.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing C. sukari requires S. mansoni for successful infection of B. pfeifferi.

claim: Most of the C. sukari infections observed in streams represent snails that had been penetrated by S. mansoni miracidia and in which some degree of schistosome sporocyst development took place.
source: This implies that most of the C. sukari infections we observed in streams represent snails that had been penetrated by S. mansoni miracidia and in which some degree of schistosome sporocyst development took place: the sporocysts were either stymied early in their development by the pre-existing presence of C. sukari larvae, or were able to develop to the point of cercariae production only to be taken over by a subsequent C. sukari infection.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental exposure data and field observations.

claim: The mathematical model predicted that C. sukari could dampen the force of transmission of S. mansoni by as much as 65 percent.
source: Specifically, our mathematical model predicted that C. sukari could dampen the force of transmission of S. mansoni by as much as 65 percent.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical modeling results.

claim: The amphistome C. sukari would not persist or would persist at much lower levels without the facilitation provided by S. mansoni.
source: Furthermore, the amphistome would not persist or would persist at much lower levels without the facilitation provided by S. mansoni.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data showing C. sukari's dependence on S. mansoni for successful infection.

claim: In current mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns in Kenya, treating humans with praziquantel would decrease the number of successful C. sukari infections in snails and in turn the number of cattle infected with C. sukari.
source: Consequently, in current mass drug administration (MDA) campaigns in Kenya, treating humans with praziquantel (with presumed downstream effects on limiting S. mansoni infections in snails) would then also decrease the number of successful C. sukari infections in snails and in turn the number of cattle infected with C. sukari.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the facilitation relationship between S. mansoni and C. sukari demonstrated experimentally.

claim: If cattle were targeted in MDA campaigns to control Fasciola gigantica and other flukes like C. sukari, assuming no concomitant S. mansoni control, an increase in the number of S. mansoni infections in snails would be expected, with the model predicting at least a 40% increase.
source: Conversely, if cattle were targeted in MDA campaigns to control Fasciola gigantica and other flukes like C. sukari, we would expect assuming no concomitant S. mansoni control, to observe an increase in the number of S. mansoni infections in snails. In particular, our model predicts at least a 40% increase (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from modeling results shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Recent transcriptional studies have indicated that S. mansoni sporocysts promote down-regulation of many B. pfeifferi immune factors, and that C. sukari transcriptomic activity may be limited without S. mansoni present.
source: Recent transcriptional studies have indicated that S. mansoni sporocysts promote down-regulation of many B. pfeifferi immune factors, and that C. sukari transcriptomic activity may be limited without S. mansoni present (Buddenborg et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published transcriptomic studies.

claim: Immune interference provided by S. mansoni enables larval development of C. sukari to proceed.
source: This is suggestive that immune interference provided by S. mansoni enables larval development of C. sukari to proceed (Lim and Heyneman, 1972).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from transcriptomic data and histological observations, supported by citation.

claim: S. mansoni and Echinostoma paraensei can interfere with Biomphalaria glabrata defenses, thereby allowing development of particular trematode strains and species that would otherwise be doomed to fail in B. glabrata.
source: Furthermore, several studies in the related snail, Biomphalaria glabrata indicate S. mansoni and Echinostoma paraensei can interfere with snail defenses, thereby allowing development of particular trematode strains and species that would otherwise be doomed to fail in B. glabrata (Lie, 1982; Lie et al., 1976; Hanington et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on immune interference in related snail species.

claim: Immune-suppression mediated by one trematode species may be a means whereby another trematode species is able to invade and colonize an otherwise incompatible snail host, thereby helping to account for high rates of snail host-switching that are a prominent feature of trematode-snail interactions.
source: We also note that immune-suppression mediated by one trematode species may be a means whereby another trematode species is able to invade and colonize an otherwise incompatible snail host, thereby helping to account for high rates of snail host-switching that are a prominent feature of trematode-snail interactions (Brant and Loker, 2013) and C. sukari may exemplify this process.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed facilitation effect and citation to literature on host-switching.

claim: S. mansoni is favored by its ability to infect diverse definitive hosts and at least three taxa of ecologically distinct Biomphalaria intermediate hosts in the hyperendemic transmission area around Lake Victoria.
source: We further note that in an area of hyperendemic transmission of S. mansoni in and around Lake Victoria, this predominantly human parasite is nonetheless favored by its ability to infect diverse definitive hosts and at least three taxa of ecologically distinct Biomphalaria intermediate hosts.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from field survey data showing multiple host species and experimental compatibility studies.

claim: The long-term use of the same snail-containing aquatic habitats by human pastoralists and their livestock has led to a situation where the parasites of cattle have seemingly been selected to exploit the predictable and widespread presence of the human parasite S. mansoni in snails.
source: The long-term use of the same snail-containing aquatic habitats by human pastoralists and their livestock has led to a situation where the parasites of cattle have seemingly been selected to exploit the predictable and widespread presence of the human parasite S. mansoni in snails.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed facilitation relationship and evolutionary reasoning about co-occurrence patterns.

claim: Pastoralism has shaped the nature of the parasites and diseases experienced by both humans and ruminants.
source: Here we show another example of how pastoralism has shaped the nature of the parasites and diseases experienced by both humans and ruminants (Greter et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the study's findings and citation to literature on pastoralism and disease.

claim: The interspecific interactions occurring between trematodes within their vector snails can have cascading effects in influencing prevalence of parasites in their definitive hosts, including humans.
source: In addition, the interspecific interactions occurring between trematodes within their vector snails can in turn have cascading effects in influencing prevalence of parasites in their definitive hosts, including humans.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the modeling results showing how within-snail interactions affect transmission to humans.

claim: Molecular markers (28S ribosomal gene, intragenic spacer ITS, cytochrome oxidase 1 cox1, and NADH dehydrogenase 1 nad1) were used to differentiate trematode species in conjunction with morphological features of the cercariae.
source: Because cryptic species commonly exist among trematodes, we employed molecular markers to more precisely differentiate species in conjunction with morphological features of the cercariae. We used both nuclear markers 28S ribosomal gene (28S) or intragenic spacer (ITS), and mitochondrial markers cytochrome oxidase 1 (cox1) or NADH dehydrogenase 1 (nad1) for this purpose.
evidence: This claim describes the methods used in the study.

claim: P-distance values less than 1.5% with respect to nad1 or cox1 genes were used to indicate samples corresponded to a single species, and values > 5% to indicate they were different species.
source: Operationally, we used p-distance values less than 1.5% with respect to nad1 or cox1 genes to indicate our samples corresponded to those of a single species, and values > 5% to indicate they were different species (Vilas et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim describes the operational criteria used for species identification, supported by citation.

claim: B. pfeifferi shed S. mansoni cercariae the earliest (4 weeks) and peaked at 6 weeks post-exposure.
source: B. pfeiffieri shed the earliest (4 weeks and peaked at 6 weeks)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental exposure data.

claim: B. sudanica and B. choanomphala started shedding S. mansoni cercariae at 6 weeks and peaked at 7 weeks post-exposure.
source: and B. sudanica and B. choanomphala started shedding at 6 weeks and peaked at 7 weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental exposure data.

claim: S. mansoni eggs were collected and pooled from five primary school children.
source: S. mansoni eggs were collected and pooled from five primary school children (see ethics statement below)
evidence: This claim describes the source of parasite material used in experiments.

claim: C. sukari eggs were harvested from cow dung samples collected along the banks of Asao stream.
source: and C. sukari eggs were harvested from cow dung samples collected along the banks of Asao stream.
evidence: This claim describes the source of parasite material used in experiments.

claim: An estimated ~10,000 C. sukari eggs are present per cowpat.
source: Domestic ruminants also predictably pass huge quantities of helminth eggs into the water, including those of C. sukari (we estimate ~10,000 eggs/cowpat).
evidence: This claim is based on estimation from field observations.

claim: The model explicitly tracks the outcomes for each parasite in the case of both simultaneous and sequential infections of B. pfeifferi with C. sukari and S. mansoni, based on survival rates from empirical data.
source: In particular, our modeling framework tracks the outcomes for each parasite in the case of both simultaneous and sequential infections of B. pfeifferi with C. sukari and S. mansoni, based on survival rates from our empirical data.
evidence: This claim describes the mathematical modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The model includes two snail size classes to account for size-dependent variation in snail survival and fecundity and cercariae output.
source: Furthermore, the model includes two snail size classes to account for size-dependent variation in snail survival and fecundity and cercariae output, which we have previously shown is important for accurately assessing the risk of infection to humans (Anderson et al., submitted).
evidence: This claim describes a feature of the mathematical model.

claim: The model includes a 'sink' snail population to account for the loss of miracidia when the larvae infect incompetent snail species that do not result in new cercariae.
source: In addition, the model includes a 'sink' snail population to account for the loss of miracidia (of both trematode species) when the larvae infect incompetent snail species that do not result in new cercariae.
evidence: This claim describes a feature of the mathematical model.
